newsitem.title: UK: Grand National to be rerun in sombre atmosphere.
newsitem.headline: Grand National to be rerun in sombre atmosphere.

text.p: From the trainer of the Epsom Derby winner to a young Liverpudlian pushing his baby in a pram, the message was the same on Monday -- they came to the Grand National to show solidarity.
They were greeted at "Fortress Aintree" by meticulous body searches at the gate. Police even checked the paddock railings with mine detectors.
British sport was paying the price after Saturday's race had to be abandoned because of an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb alert.
The carnival atmosphere of one of the country's biggest sporting events was replaced by a sombre mood of reflection among crowds watched every step of the way by security staff.
Prime Minister John Major and Princess Anne were on hand to watch the race and the Gurkha band tried to raise the spirit of the crowd on the 150th anniversary of the world's most famous steeplechase.
Setting up his satchel and board, bookmaker George Horne summed up the mood: "There is a macabre feeling here with a bit of morbid curiosity thrown in."

Horne, one of about 20 bookmakers doing modest business along the rails, confessed: "It does feel a bit weird. It has the feeling of a non-event. The atmosphere and excitement have gone. They are just running it as a matter of principle."

Peter O'Sullevan, the "Voice of British racing," commentating on the race for his 50th and final time, agreed: "It is less charismatic. A certain amount of drama always associated with it has been dissipated by this painful interim."
Leading trainers from Newmarket, the home of British flat racing, made the 500 mile (800 kilometre) round trip from eastern England to show solidarity.
"I have never been here before and felt it was important to show team spirit," said William Haggas, who trained the 1996 Epsom Derby winner Shaamit.
Liverpudlians queued for an hour outside to get into the races for a free day out. Once inside, they were told over the loudspeaker: "Do not leave any bags unattended. Remain vigilant at all times."
Terry White, wheeling his eight-month-old daughter Jade, said: "I came because it was free, I wanted to see the horses in the flesh and show the IRA we won't be beaten."
The jockeys had trouble pumping themselves up for the tingling ordeal of riding over some of the toughest fences in the world.
"I like having one or two races to get warmed up but today is something different. Adrenalin alone will keep us going," said dual National winning jockey Richard Dunwoody.
